title_en: A Trance of Devotion (Bhava-Samadhi) in Jagannath Puri
translation:
On hearing this sakhi, Jivanji Maharaj felt great joy, and understanding that this was some meritorious soul, he placed his hand upon her head — and at once her disability left her. Seeing this, Harmaba's father, Ratansinh, said, "I offer my daughter to you." Hearing this, Jivanji Maharaj said that they were wanderers who roamed from land to land, and that this would not befit a life of renunciation. The other devotees of the Guru who were present then persuaded Jivandasji.

Word of this also reached Gopaldasji in Chorenda, and he too said that this was indeed the wish of the Gracious Lord — that he should enter into worldly life (grihasth ashram). Jivandasji then agreed. Harmaba, moreover, said:

_Tumkun chhod avar kahaan jaau, nishadin tumhaari sang rahaavun._
(Leaving You, where else could I go? Day and night I shall remain in Your company.)

Hearing these words of Harmaba, he accepted her — just as Jagannath Swami had once given Padmavati to Jaydevji. In this way, by Hari's will, he accepted Harmaba, and himself stayed on for one month, singing hari-kirtan. He gave everyone knowledge (upadesh/teaching) and dispelled their ignorance. He then told Harmaba, "I shall travel with Gopaldasji through Malwa, Jagannathji, Naimisharanya, Kashi, Ayodhya, Mathura, and Badrikashram, and when I return I shall take care of you" — and having said this, he himself departed for Chorenda.

Bhava-Samadhi in Jagannath Puri

By the command of Guru Gopaldasji, Jivanji Maharaj set out with him from Chorenda toward Malwa on the tenth day of the bright half of Aso, in Vikram Samvat 1687. But in Malwa, since the financial condition of Gopaldasji's friend was not sufficient to support both guru and disciple, Jivanji Maharaj sought leave from Guru Gopaldas and travelled on ahead alone. On the way, afflicted by hunger, Jivanji Maharaj ate the fruit of the beheda tree. Having eaten too much of the fruit,

he became intoxicated by it and fell unconscious, remaining so for some time beneath that very tree. At this time, a company of saints happened to be passing on their way to pilgrimage at Jagannath Puri; they saw Jivanji Maharaj lying unconscious, and this company of saints then brought him along with them to Jagannath Puri. He remained there for some days. One evening, in the presence of Lord Jagannath, Jivanji Maharaj slipped into bhava-samadhi (a trance of devotional absorption), losing all awareness of time. In this state he remained seated, leaning against a pillar. As night fell, the temple's attendants and priests closed the temple doors and went home.

Jivanji Maharaj lay absorbed in bhava-samadhi, with no awareness of time at all. At midnight, hearing the sound of someone moving about on every side, he awoke from his trance and began looking around, only to realize that he was shut inside the temple. He could see no one, yet he heard the sound of someone's footsteps. This episode in the life of Jivanji Maharaj —
